justice: The street provides a relatively wide paved corridor that can be used by multiple users, but much of the right-of-way is occupied by parked cars on the right side.
Ground-floor shops line the left edge, offering access to daily services, yet storefront spillover elements such as signs, mats, and potted decorations narrow the pedestrian edge.
No clearly marked barrier-free path, tactile paving, or dedicated separated pedestrian zone is visible, so accessibility is only moderate for the full range of users.
safety: Pedestrians, scooters, and cars appear to share the same paved space without strong vertical or painted separation, increasing conflict risk.
Angle and parallel parking along the right side create reversing and door-opening hazards in the main circulation area.
Traffic cones and small parking locks in the center of the pavement suggest ad hoc traffic management rather than a clearly organized safe street layout.
livability: The row of active ground-floor commercial storefronts on the left supports daily convenience and creates some street activity.
Trees and green space along the right edge improve environmental quality and soften the otherwise hard paved setting.
The space lacks visible benches, social seating, or dedicated gathering areas, which limits its function as a comfortable public place beyond access and parking.
sustainability: The trees and planted green strip on the right contribute some ecological value and shade potential.
A very large proportion of the visible space is hard pavement used for vehicle access and parking, which weakens stormwater and heat-mitigation performance.
No dedicated bike lane, bus stop, rain garden, or other obvious low-carbon or green-infrastructure feature is visible in the scene.
aesthetics: The building row has a consistent height and material palette, giving the street a coherent visual frame.
Storefront signage is colorful and active, but the mix of signs, external air-conditioning units, and parked vehicles creates visual clutter.
The trees on the right add welcome greenery and improve the view, though the space still reads more like a service lane than a designed civic street.
comfort: The paving appears generally smooth and level, which supports basic physical comfort for walking and rolling.
Shade is uneven: the trees on the right provide some cover, but much of the central paved area and storefront edge remains exposed to sun.
The absence of benches or resting amenities reduces overall comfort, and shared movement with cars and scooters can lower psychological comfort.
walkability: The route is wide and paved, but there is no clearly protected sidewalk separated from vehicle movement.
Parked cars, scooters near storefronts, cones, and parking devices interrupt the clarity of the walking path.
Active shopfronts make the edge more interesting for pedestrians, yet the space functions primarily as a mixed access and parking lane rather than a pedestrian-priority street.
bikeability: No dedicated bicycle lane or protected cycling facility is visible anywhere in the corridor.
Cyclists would need to mix with cars, parked vehicles, and scooters in a constrained shared space.
There is no visible bicycle parking, bike markings, or intersection treatment to support convenient and legible cycling.
